title: Russell goes fastest in busy final practice at Monza
excerpt:
George Russell ended a busy final practice session at the Italian Grand Prix on top of the timesheets, the Mercedes driver going fastest ahead of Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and the Red Bull of Max Verstappen.

In what would prove to be an action-packed hour, Russell worked his way down to a 1m 22.219s to maintain his momentum after leading the way in Friday’s second practice.

It was a quiet start to Saturday’s session when the green light appeared at 1230 local time, with the Audi pair of Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg initially having the track to themselves during the opening moments before the Alpines joined the action soon afterwards.

Meanwhile there was early trouble for Alex Albon, who reported an issue with his steering wheel that saw his car wheeled back into the Williams garage. As the action picked up, the problem appeared to have been resolved as the Thai driver joined other drivers on an increasingly busy track.

Pierre Gasly had gone fastest after the opening 15 minutes, with many of the frontrunning cars still to head out. Elsewhere, Ferrari sent Charles Leclerc and Hamilton out a few minutes later in a welcome sight for the watching Tifosi, both cars sporting the soft tyres.

Kimi Antonelli soon shot to the top of the timesheets, the Mercedes driver setting a lap of 1m 23.032s on a weekend in which he will start from the back of the field due to a grid penalty for a planned engine change.

The yellow flags were briefly thrown when Liam Lawson suffered a spin into the first chicane, the Red Bull driver reporting struggles with “the rear in low speed”. Albon, meanwhile, had been issued with a warning for failing to follow the Race Director’s instructions regarding the escape road.

Antonelli remained on top as the final practice hour reached its halfway point, the Italian two tenths clear of Leclerc while Gasly followed in third. Other drivers sounded less happy, with Oscar Piastri having to take to the escape road after a lock-up into the first corner before sarcastically commenting that things were “great”.

Russell was the next to go fastest on a 1m 22.697s, going three tenths quicker than his team mate – but the Briton still had to contend with traffic soon afterwards, radioing in that there was nothing he could do after getting caught up in a group of cars.

As the final 15 minutes of the session ticked down, the likes of Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen were amongst the first to bolt on fresh soft tyres for their closing laps, leading to a flurry of quicker times going on the board.

Meanwhile Williams were utilising the power of the tow, with Albon – who, like Antonelli, will start from the back due to engine penalties – towing Carlos Sainz in a move that they will be hoping to gain from later in Qualifying. Separately, it was confirmed that both drivers will be investigated after the session for a yellow flag infringement.

Elsewhere Verstappen was voicing his annoyance after feeling that a Ferrari was “always in the way” ahead of him amid a very busy track. Russell had been noted for potentially impeding Piastri, before the stewards decided that no further investigation was necessary.

There was a feisty moment between former title rivals Hamilton and Verstappen, with Hamilton overtaking before the pair went side-by-side down the main straight and engaged in a tense moment into Turn 2, sparking unhappy comments from both on the radio. The incident was noted by the stewards, but it was subsequently not investigated.

Ultimately Russell remained on top with his effort of 1m 22.219s, two tenths clear of Hamilton in second with Verstappen third. Antonelli placed in fourth, with McLaren’s Lando Norris fifth and Leclerc sixth, while Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad, Piastri, Gasly and the sister Alpine of Franco Colapinto completing the top 10.

Hulkenberg was 11th ahead of Lawson, Bortoleto, Haas’ Ollie Bearman, Yuki Tsunoda in the Racing Bulls, Sainz, the other Haas of Esteban Ocon and Albon. At the back of the order were the Aston Martins of Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll in 19th and 22nd respectively, with the Cadillacs of Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez separating them.

With the final practice hour complete, the attentions of the Monza paddock will now switch to Qualifying, which is set to get underway at 1600 local time.

title: Outstanding Kato claims maiden F3 victory in Monza Sprint Race
excerpt:
Taito Kato went from ninth on the grid to victory with a brilliant drive in the Formula 3 Monza Sprint Race.

The ART Grand Prix driver picked off his rivals one by one before holding off TRIDENT’s Freddie Slater for the final two laps to win at the Temple of Speed.

Championship leader Slater went from 12th on the grid to second, as he extends his lead to 17 points going into the Feature Race.

Van Amersfoort Racing’s Hiyu Yamakoshi took the final place on the podium, with AIX Racing’s Yevan David’s final lap overtake on Alessandro Giusti putting him fourth.

Giusti had led for most of the race but settled for P5 ahead of his MP Motorsport team mate Mattia Colnaghi, with Campos Racing’s Ernesto Rivera in seventh.

Van Amersfoort Racing’s Enzo Deligny finished eighth ahead of DAMS Lucas Oil’s Nicola Lacorte with his team mate Bruno del Pino rounding out the points in P10.

Slater is set to start from pole position in Sunday’s Feature Race, with ART driver Kanato Le set to join him on the front row.

title: Formula 2 unveils new car for 2027 and beyond
excerpt:
Formula 2 has unveiled its latest challenger for the 2027, 2028 and 2029 seasons in a bespoke event held in the paddock at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza.

The support championship has offered many drivers the opportunity to showcase their talents with the ambition of landing a full-time seat in Formula 1, with recent graduates including current standings leader Kimi Antonelli, Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad.

F2 has fully embraced that role through the creation of its new car, which features redesigned front and rear wings and the addition of an on-board starter to further evolve the championship, prepare racers for the top tier and encourage closer racing.

It also aligns F2 with the current F1 design philosophy, while retaining the current Dallara chassis to manage costs and continuing to use advanced sustainable fuel supplied by Aramco, as well as Pirelli tyres.

Furthermore, the 2027 car will still be accessible to a wide range of drivers thanks to its unchanged specifications for braking performance, steering effort and cockpit ergonomics.

Stefano Domenicali, President & CEO of Formula 1, said: “Formula 2 is the ultimate proving ground for the next generation of Formula 1 drivers, where the very best young talent competes wheel-to-wheel and develops the skills needed to reach the pinnacle of motorsport.

“This new car is another important step forward, combining innovation, safety and closer racing while maintaining the level playing field that allows drivers to showcase their ability.

“I want to thank His Excellency Mohammed Ben Sulayem and the FIA, Bruno Michel and his team, plus all the technical partners and teams whose collaboration has made this possible. We look forward to seeing the car on the grid, and watching this talented generation create their own stories as they fight for the opportunity to make their mark in Formula 1.”

Bruno Michel, FIA Formula 2 Championship CEO, added: “When working on this new car, our first goal was to ensure it remains the perfect tool to prepare drivers for F1.

“Together with the FIA, we have opted for the current chassis and focused on redesigning the front and the rear wings. This enables us to keep the costs managed, while bringing the design closer to the look of an F1 car while enhancing the F2 car’s ability to deliver close racing.

“We have added an on-board starter that will simplify the operational side for the teams and will allow the drivers to restart their car after spinning or stalling on track, and we’ve been continuing our work with our partners Aramco and Pirelli on driver preparation, sustainability, and providing the fans with a great show.

“Our fans expect the F2 races to be highly entertaining and safe, and this new kit will deliver exactly that.”

title: When Schumacher retired after winning in front of the Tifosi
excerpt:
Twenty years ago, as the sounds of the Tifosi could be heard from outside of the press conference walls, Michael Schumacher announced his (first) retirement from Formula 1, fresh from winning the 2006 Italian Grand Prix.

It was an emotional and defining moment, as the seven-time World Champion made a heartfelt statement to fans after lots of speculation, bringing an end to the most successful partnership F1 fans had ever seen at that point.

It’s often said that Ferrari is like another religion to some. It’s the product of passion, resilience, courage and identity, all wrapped up in a beautiful and unmistakable red livery. It’s the stuff dreams are made of – and one man who is synonymous with the Scuderia is Schumacher.

Changing the opinion of the Tifosi

When Schumacher joined Ferrari in 1996, he was a well-established entity in F1. With two drivers’ titles under his belt from his time at Benetton, and clearly a generational talent, the Schumacher-hype was high – yet when he joined the Scuderia, some fans were still not sold on the idea.

Schumacher was clear from the start that there was work to do at Ferrari, explaining that “this is the kind of motivation that I was looking for” and that he wasn’t after an “easy job, where I sit in the car and I win every race or people expect me to win every race.”

Then came the 1996 Spanish Grand Prix, where Schumacher took his first win in that famous shade of red during torrential rain.

It’s often regarded as one of his finest victories, and was a real showcase of his talents. It gave the Tifosi a real insight into the future of Ferrari, and later that year, he’d also win in Belgium and Italy, with the latter being a real turning point for the fans and Schumacher himself.

Ferrari had won in Italy before – 10 times before Schumacher’s ‘96 achievement – but this was different. Before his signing, the Prancing Horse had won just twice in the last five seasons and the Tifosi’s belief was at a low, but now things were on the up and a victory in front of the team’s home crowd was a huge turning point.

“I have never seen so many emotions,” Schumacher said in the press conference after the win, “so many people enjoying themselves. It’s fantastic, and you can only see that in Italy.”

From there, Schumacher kept winning. He was able to help build an organisation around him that brought the team into a new generation. Alongside Team Principal Jean Todt, he snapped up two former Benetton colleagues, Technical Director Ross Brawn and recently-retired Chief Designer Rory Byrne, and from there kept adding to the Maranello trophy cabinet.

Today, the Schumacher name is synonymous with Ferrari. His legacy from his time at that team, taking an astounding 72 wins whilst with the Italian constructor, will forever see the two as one of Formula 1’s greatest pairings.

Revisit Schumacher's first Ferrari win in the torrential rain of the 1996 Spanish GP

“Michael brought back the respect Ferrari needed,” Brawn said in a recent interview with Ferrari. “Before that era, success was expected, but not always earned. Michael changed that.

“The achievements, and the way they were achieved, restored enormous pride inside the factory and renewed the respect people had for Ferrari outside it. He lifted Ferrari to a new level and made people feel proud to be part of the organisation. If I had to summarise his legacy, it would be that.”

It’s that heritage that fans, and the Scuderia themselves, still chase today. The Tifosi are some of the most energetic and enthusiastic followers in all of sports, and will flock to Monza in their tens of thousands.

Wearing red, whether that’s team gear or their own designs, you’ll struggle to find a grandstand at the Italian Grand Prix that isn’t plastered in national flags, images of the Prancing Horse, and hand-written banners. It’s an incredibly serious love that runs deep through generations.

Why Monza is magic

Although the Imola circuit is closer to Ferrari’s Maranello base, Monza has always felt like the home event for Ferrari as the host of the Italian Grand Prix. It’s nicknamed the Temple of Speed, but it's also a temple of sorts for the Tifosi. Winning here in red is every Ferrari driver’s dream, and it’s one Schumacher managed on multiple occasions.

That first one in 1996 was special for a variety of reasons, but it was followed by another win in 1998, with Schumacher's then-team mate Eddie Irvine making it a Ferrari 1-2 in front of the waves of passionate Italians. More first-place finishes from pole came in 2000 and 2003.

Then came 2006, and Michael’s final win at the Temple of Speed. He started second, took the lead during a smart pit stop strategy, and cruised to the finish line in first, much to the delight of the Tifosi. As he stood on top of the podium, joined by Jean Todt, the crowd below cheered their hero, but just minutes later Schumacher announced his retirement from racing.

Ferrari reveal special Schumacher-inspired livery for home Grand Prix at Monza

It was the perfect place to do it, fresh from victory and with the full support of the Tifosi surrounding him in a beautiful bubble. Monza became a place for Schumacher to physically feel and see how much people worshipped him for the golden years.

It was that relationship with the historic circuit that makes it the perfect place for The Schumacher Lounge, a dedicated hospitality experience that is held in collaboration with Schumacher’s family and the Keep Fighting foundation.

“Michael Schumacher’s relationship with Ferrari became something far greater than that of a driver and a team,” James O'Brien, co-founder of The Schumacher Lounge in Monza, said about the iconic racer.

“The Italian fans recognised something in Michael. His absolute commitment, his relentless pursuit of perfection and his willingness to carry the enormous weight of Ferrari’s expectations made him one of their own. His victories at Monza became much more than sporting achievements. They were shared moments between Schumacher and the Tifosi, and that connection remains incredibly powerful today.”

Of course, Schumacher couldn’t stay away and returned to racing with Mercedes for three seasons, with his final podium being at the 2012 European Grand Prix in Valencia.

title: Why Alonso still backs Honda '100%' after tough Monza practice
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix weekend was always going to be a big test for Aston Martin and Honda given the obvious focus on straight line performance, and after the boost of Fernando Alonso’s hard-earned P9 in Zandvoort everyone in the camp was aware that Monza could be something of a reality check.

Indeed at the end of Friday’s FP2 session the quickest AMR26 of Alonso was down in P19, 2.468s off the quickest time of George Russell. Only the two Cadillacs and his team mate Lance Stroll were behind him, and perhaps most telling was the gap to the rest of the midfield, as Fernando was 1.174s shy of the quickest Williams.

It was a clear sign that Honda’s revised power unit has yet to demonstrate the sort of gains that the team needs to see, despite efforts to address the driveability issues that were apparent both on its race debut at Zandvoort and also at the Budapest filming day that preceded it.

“Obviously we knew it was going to be a difficult Friday, a difficult weekend for us,” Aston Martin’s Pedro de la Rosa said after FP2. “It's more or less what we were expecting after all the work we carried out in the simulator. So yes, it's tough. But on the positive note, we went through the programme quite well, and we managed to try everything we were planning to.

“We shouldn't be surprised about where we are because we knew beforehand, and we said that yesterday – the drivers said that that it was going to be difficult for us. It's very circuit specific at the moment, so there will be some circuits that are better than others, and definitely Monza was one of those that we were not looking forward to.”

Honda learned some useful lessons in Zandvoort, and the need to improve driveability was reflected in a focus on combustion changes ahead of Monza.

“We have observed a step forward in terms of performance on our metrics, as expected,” Honda's Trackside General Manager and Chief Engineer Shintaro Orihara said of the Dutch GP.

“We have confirmed on the dyno, so that was positive, things we found in the Netherlands. But on the other hand, we found something which can improve on drivability. We have updated combustion characteristics, and then we prepared a data setting to adapt to new combustion to get better drivability.”

'More to come' from Aston Martin - Alonso feeling 'very positive' after upgrades

Orihara noted after FP2 that the countermeasures were working well, although the lap times told their own story about how far Honda has to go in order to get on a par with the other manufacturers.

Despite the ongoing frustrations Alonso has faith that the company will return to the level that saw it win World Championships with Red Bull.

“One hundred percent, yes,” the Spaniard said on Thursday. “I think it's a huge commitment from Honda. The facilities we have in Japan are one of the best. I think the personnel and the management of the power unit now has been reinforced, as Honda said, and a lot of people that were in the previous project they are in again on this one. I think I have no doubts, and I trust one hundred percent Honda.

“We just need to shortcut somehow that process. Unfortunately, we started with the wrong foot, and we started with this set of regulations, not at the level that we wanted. But I have no doubts that they will get there.

“And as I said many times, we don't want to wait, you know, five years like they did last time, or six years. We want to do it in two years or three years maximum.”

The Zandvoort result was a welcome boost for the team after a tough season, but Alonso is under no illusions.

“Obviously, we cannot be happy with P9, and I think no one is happy in the team,” the two-time World Champion said. “It was a nice boost for everyone, knowing that at least the direction that we are taking is the right one, because we changed a lot of things in the car since Budapest, and obviously we know or we feel that in the corners we are getting, you know, in a much better place.

“So that gives hope for everyone in Silverstone that if we keep on going on this philosophy and this strategy and this pace of development, eventually we will be one of the fastest on the corners. So we tick one of the boxes.

“Then on the engine side, I think Zandvoort was not a big improvement, to be honest. The driveability was a problem, and the extra power was difficult to feel in Zandvoort.

“Maybe Monza is going to be a truer test for the engine, but still a long way to go, and we need to improve in both ends, in chassis and on engine for next year, and it's a must.”

title: Ferrari pole at Italian GP 'ultimate dream' – Hamilton
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton admits the prospect of pole position for this weekend's Italian Grand Prix in front of Ferrari's home fans is "the ultimate dream", as he and team mate Charles Leclerc enjoyed a strong Friday.

The Tifosi were left thrilled after the opening hour of practice at Monza, as Leclerc headed Hamilton at the top of the times, before the pair slipped to P2 and P5 respectively in the second session.

Hamilton later explained that his deficit in Free Practice 2, which stood at nearly half a second to George Russell's Mercedes, was partly due to not having a tow down Monza's long straights.

"The long run wasn’t bad, just lacking a bit of pace," said Hamilton. "But a lot of the pace came from straight-line speed, a lot to do with tows and stuff. I was pretty on my own out there.

"But the Mercedes is very quick on the straights as always, so we have some work to do overnight to see if we can improve that and improve the balance a little bit.

"It’s going to be tight, it is very close. We are up against the McLarens and the Mercedes, they both look very, very competitive.

"Every weekend, the Mercedes is just really, really quick. It will be tough for sure, but we really need to knuckle down tonight and see if we can pull something out."

Hamilton has enjoyed a resurgence in form during his sophomore season with Ferrari, which included his first Grand Prix victory for the Scuderia in Barcelona.

The seven-time World Champion sits joint-second in the drivers' standings, 59 points behind Kimi Antonelli, and has yet to take a pole position in red – admitting that doing it in front of the team's home fans would be special.

"I mean, that’s the dream, that’s the ultimate dream. Whether or not we can is the big, big question," he said.

"It is going to take a lot of work tonight to try and figure out if we have gone wrong anywhere and if there’s any places we can improve.

"There are loads of places we can improve, but as I said, being in the right place at the right time on this track is going to help a lot."

title: Lawson and Red Bull assess 'productive' Friday in Italy
excerpt:
Liam Lawson believes Red Bull had a "productive day" during Friday practice ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, despite neither himself nor team mate Max Verstappen challenging the leading contenders.

The New Zealander will race for Red Bull again this weekend having competed with the team in Zandvoort as a stand-in for Isack Hadjar, who continues to recover from a broken wrist.

Lawson managed to finish Free Practice 1 fourth in Italy, four tenths adrift of the top time, before only finishing P12 later in the afternoon as he focused on long runs.

"It was okay. It's been, I would say, a productive day. We spent most of FP2 doing long running," said Lawson, who finished P7 in the Netherlands after his switch from Racing Bulls.

"We did a short run at the start and felt okay, and then we just did two long runs on the soft and hard [tyre]. For me, it's good learning. I think I struggled more in Zandvoort in the race versus Qualifying, so I will try and learn what I can from it."

Verstappen finished FP2 in ninth, having missed the opening, one-hour session of practice as his Red Bull was driven by the team's reserve driver and rookie, Ayumu Iwasa.

The four-time World Champion suffered with bouncing during his running, as well as replacing his front wing at one stage, with Technical Director Pierre Wache admitting the team had work to do overnight in a bid to close the gap to the leading teams.

"We discovered some other issues with the car during FP2, especially on his car that we have to try and understand during this evening and for sure, fix for tomorrow," he said.

"We try to close the gap to the top. Normally on one lap, we are a little bit behind and on a long run, it's a little bit better but difficult to say. Everybody in the team is trying to close this gap for sure."

title: How young Max Verstappen left karting boss stunned
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's old karting boss has opened up on what the Dutchman was truly like at the start of his career.

Giancarlo Tinini, the Italian owner of karting manufacturer CRG, has offered a rare insight into the early years of Max Verstappen, recalling the moment he first laid eyes on the four-time world champion and immediately recognised something special.

Speaking to De Telegraaf from Monza, where he was attending as a guest of the Verstappen family, Tinini reflected on what set the Red Bull driver apart from an exceptionally young age.

"What stands out most in my mind is Max's enormous drive to race," Tinini said. "He always wanted to push the limits, in every situation.

"Even when he was very young, he was already incredibly professional and completely focused on what he was doing. You could clearly see that he wasn't just there to drive a few laps. He always wanted to understand how he could go even faster."

Verstappen signed a factory contract with CRG in November 2009, with Tinini already having an existing relationship with the family before the deal was formalised.

"I already knew his father and mother, so there was already a connection," he said. "Max has been one of CRG's best ambassadors.

"We're all very proud that he was part of our team and of what we've achieved together."

Driver

First meeting with Verstappen

For Tinini, 2013 stands as the defining chapter of their time together. "That was the year 2013," Tinini added. "Max won two European championships and a world title that year.

"He was fighting for another world championship, in the KF class, but that was derailed after a collision. All in all, though, it was a fantastic season. A wonderful way to wrap things up."

The CRG owner also revealed that, despite his existing ties to the Verstappen family, he had no prior knowledge of Max when he first saw him on track. The impression, however, was instant.

"I can still remember that [the first time] very well," Tinini said. "Max was still too young to officially compete in an international race. I saw a CRG kart on the track with the number 3, without any real stickers, just the name 'Max.'"

"I had no idea who it was, but I was impressed by what he showed. I wanted to find out who he was right away, ran into Jos, and asked if he was one of his drivers.

"Jos said, 'Well, no, this is my son.' Max was still very young, but I immediately asked if they were interested in joining our team. It was pretty clear right away just how talented he was."

title: George Russell throws down Ferrari Monza pole challenge as Lewis Hamilton nearest rival
excerpt:
It is George Russell who emerged fastest from the final practice session from the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

George Russell is the favourite for Italian Grand Prix pole position, with Lewis Hamilton emerging as his closest rival in Free Practice 3.

In the final 60 minutes at Monza, Russell clocked a 1:22.219 to top his second session of the weekend, after FP2, with Hamilton's Ferrari slotting in 0.226s behind.

Max Verstappen rounded out the top three in an otherwise tight session as just over two-tenths seperated Hamilton in second and Arvid Lindblad in seventh.

Qualifying starts later this afternoon at 15:00 local time, 14:00 BST.

With drivers keen to find the precious tow and slipstream to aid lap times, most of the action was centred around the second half of the session, with Kimi Antonelli topping the initial times, although he will carry a 30-place grid penalty for an engine change.

Russell ultimately topped the times on a 1:22.219, being aided by the tow from Antonelli through Curva Grande and into Turn 4, with Hamilton getting the tow from the McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

title: 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix - Monza Free Practice 3 results
excerpt:
George Russell continued his fine form at the Italian Grand Prix, comfortably topping the final free practice session at Monza, over two-tenths clear of Lewis Hamilton.

Max Verstappen rounded out the top three, whilst Kimi Antonelli and Lando Norris completed the top five at the Temple of Speed.

Despite Russell's electric pace giving him a seemingly comfortable buffer heading into qualifying, where his penalty-bound team-mate will be aiding his efforts, the fight for second place is close, with only three more tenths down to eighth.

It was another relatively quiet session, with Liam Lawson spinning at the first chicane one of the standout moments from the third hour of practice running.

Oscar Piastri was particularly grumpy, taking to team radio on multiple occasions to vent his frustration at traffic and the difficulties he encountered getting an adequate tow for his qualifying simulations. The McLaren driver ended up eighth, after Russell ruined his penultimate effort.

Verstappen and Hamilton proved that there is no love lost between them in the dying moments. After the Ferrari driver cheekily snuck by into the final corner before their last push laps, the Dutchman dive-bombed him into Turn 1, scuppering both their attempts. The two drivers were noted by the stewards for the episode but not further action was taken.

Both Williams drivers are under investigation for potential yellow flag infringements, after Alex Albon was also handed a warning for incorrectly using an escape road.

title: Cadillac handed heavy fine as F1 teams warned of stronger penalties
excerpt:
Cadillac has been handed a €30,000 fine, €25,000 of which is suspended by F1 stewards for a rules breach after Colton Herta stopped on track during Free Practice 1 - and also warned teams of possible future sporting sanctions.

The American was deputising for Sergio Perez in his third FP1 outing of the season when he stopped exiting the second Lesmo corner with about 40 minutes remaining in the session.

Although he had stopped by a marshal's post, the session was upgraded from a virtual safety car to a red flag after the MAC-26 machine could not be moved with the clutch still engaged, with the team describing the problem as a hydraulics issue.

Herta was subsequently called to the stewards over an alleged breach of Article C9.3 of the technical regulations

This states that "all cars must be fitted with a means of disengaging the clutch for a minimum of 15 minutes in the event of the car coming to rest with the engine stopped" and that this must be “in working order throughout the Competition even if the main hydraulic, pneumatic or electrical systems on the car have failed."

In Canada, Racing Bulls was handed a €30,000 fine, €20,000 of which was suspended for 12 months, following a similar breach of Article C9.3 by Liam Lawson.

In Monaco, McLaren received a similar sanction after Lando Norris's car failed in practice and was unable to be moved.

In judging against Cadillac and Herta, with the hearing delayed until Saturday morning to allow the team more time to gather data and information, the stewards found that a third-party part failure had caused the issue - and warned that after the third CDS failure of the season, sporting penalties could soon be handed out.

The Stewards heard from the team Sporting Director and team Head of Reliability, and the FIA Technical Delegate and FIA F1 Electronics Engineer.

The team presented detailed schematics of how the CDS system was designed and installed.

The Stewards were satisfied that the system was designed to operate independently of the car’s other systems, as required by the regulations.

The team demonstrated to the Stewards’ satisfaction, that the system had been checked and tested on the day prior to the commencement of competition. However the operation of the CDS when the car’s electronic system is turned off (“P0 mode”) depends on a lithium battery provided by a third party supplier.

The team was able to demonstrate, again to the Stewards’ satisfaction, that one of the four cells in this battery had failed. This in turn caused the CDS to be inoperable and hence when the car came to a halt, it could not be easily pushed from the circuit, resulting in the display of a red flag.

The team stated that as a result of the incident it would firstly obtain from the battery supplier, information as to the expected maximum battery life, and would instigate daily or pre-session checks, plus a replacement battery programme to ensure the likelihood of future failures was minimised.

The FIA Regulations state: “This system must be in working order throughout the Competition even if the main hydraulic, pneumatic or electrical systems on the car have failed.”

The Stewards accept that the team has been completely transparent in its disclosures and that the plan outlined above is a reasonable approach. However a breach of the regulation has occurred, and although the reason for this can be attributed to the failure of a third party supplied part, overall responsibility for compliance still rests with the team and accordingly a penalty is imposed.

The Stewards note that this is the third reported failure of a CDS this season. Again, this failure resulted in a red flag being displayed which had sporting consequences.

Although in this case the Stewards have decided to impose a monetary penalty, Competitors are advised that because the CDS is a critical component and designed to facilitate the safe and quick removal of a car from the circuit, future failures may incur not only monetary penalties but sporting penalties as well.

title: Haas explain difficult dilemma in giving new F1 engine to one driver
excerpt:
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu has explained the difficult dilemma the team faced in deciding which driver received Ferrari's new ADUO-boosted engine for the Italian Grand Prix.

The team receives its power units from Ferrari, with the rules dictating that, should an ADUO-upgrade-boosted engine be available for the works team, one example should be made open to each customer squad.

When Ferrari introduced its previous ADUO-upgraded engine in Barcelona, Haas elected to wait until both Oliver Bearman and Esteban Ocon could access the new unit, but given the power sensitivity at Monza, the team has decided to give Bearman the nod in using the new engine.

Explaining the decision not to give it to Ocon, Komatsu explained the factors evaluated and how it was Bearman's turn.

"Customers need to have 'A' unit," Komatsu confirmed to media, including RacingNews365, about the rules around customer teams receiving their ADUO-boosted power units.

"The last time around we didn't [give it to one driver]; we waited until we had enough engines to introduce it for both drivers together. But this time, Monza is a very power-sensitive circuit, so it's a shame to have performance sitting in a garage, right?

"It would have been better if two engines were available at least, but Ferrari's pushing like hell to get as much performance on the engine as possible. Of course, they want to introduce it at Monza, right? But that means they got the minimum quantity, so it is just to satisfy the regulation."

When then asked how the decision had been made to give the engine to Bearman, Komatsu detailed how Ocon had received early upgrades.

"It's not an aerodynamic upgrade, like items we had such as a CI brakes test, and Esteban was struggling more with brakes, so considering the Montreal upgrade we gave to Ollie, we decided to give the brake upgrade to Esteban first, and in terms of the power steering, we had another upgrade in Budapest.

"We decided to give that to Esteban because he was more vocal about it and he was struggling more on the power steering, so the last upgrade we gave to Esteban, and this time, it was Ollie.

"There's no point bullshitting, right? We operate as transparently as possible, and of course you can't please everyone every time, but we don't have any hidden agenda.

"We don't have any personal agenda for one driver or another. So we've been building that relationship. Perhaps of course, Esteban won't be happy not to get the power unit number four straight away. But this is the best for the team, and then this is the fairest way you can do it.

"But then nothing is completely fair, right? So all you can do is be transparent and upfront about it."

title: F2 unveils new car for 2027 season and beyond
excerpt:
The new F2 car, which will be used from 2027 to 2029, has been unveiled ahead of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

The previous iteration has been in use for the past three years, with the current cycle coming to an end upon the conclusion of the campaign, which is currently being led by Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov.

As the senior-most support category for F1, Formula 2 machinery is vitally important to the continued development of young drivers as they ascend the feeder ladder to the pinnacle of motorsport, or other leading championships, such as Formula E, WEC and IndyCar.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "Formula 2 is where the next generation of top drivers are made. The new 2027 car raises the bar on safety, delivers closer racing, improves accessibility, and reinforces our commitment to sustainability.

"Developed with Formula 2 and our technical partners, this car is designed to push young drivers and prepare them for the highest level of competition, while providing fans with even better racing. It is a key step in strengthening the FIA's single-seater pathway and developing the champions of tomorrow."

The series describes the new model as a significant evolution of the current generation, and while the 2027 car retains the existing Dallara chassis in a move designed to control costs, several aerodynamic changes have been introduced.

Redesigned front and rear wings are intended to improve the car's ability to follow more closely, potentially allowing for closer and more competitive racing.

The revised appearance also brings the F2 car more in line with Formula 1's latest design philosophy, further strengthening the championship's position as the final step on the single-seater ladder before F1.

"Formula 2 is the ultimate proving ground for the next generation of Formula 1 drivers, where the very best young talent competes wheel-to-wheel and develops the skills needed to reach the pinnacle of motorsport," Stefano Domenicali, F1 president and CEO, added.

"This new car is another important step forward, combining innovation, safety and closer racing while maintaining the level playing field that allows drivers to showcase their ability.

"I want to thank Mohammed Ben Sulayem and the FIA, Bruno Michel and his team, plus all the technical partners and teams whose collaboration has made this possible.

"We look forward to seeing the car on the grid, and watching this talented generation create their own stories as they fight for the opportunity to make their mark in Formula 1."

Into the details

The new car will continue to use Mecachrome's 3.4-litre turbocharged engine, while sustainable fuel supplied by Aramco will remain part of the package after being introduced to the championship in 2025.

Pirelli will also continue as F2's exclusive tyre supplier, providing tyres developed specifically for the series.

One of the most notable technical additions for the new version is an on-board starter. The feature has required an evolution of the current gearbox to be developed to accommodate the integrated starter system.

Elsewhere, the car retains the FIA's 2024 specifications covering braking performance, steering effort and cockpit ergonomics, maintaining accessibility for a wide range of drivers.

The existing Marelli electronic and hydraulic systems will also carry over, including the EM Motorsport Marshalling system.

With the current car having established itself as an important platform for drivers preparing for Formula 1, the 2027 challenger represents an evolution rather than a wholesale redesign as FIA Formula 2 looks to continue refining the final stage of the pathway to F1.

Bruno Michel, FIA Formula 2 Championship CEO, said: "When working on this new car, our first goal was to ensure it remains the perfect tool to prepare drivers for F1.

"Together with the FIA, we have opted for the current chassis and focused on redesigning the front and the rear wings. This enables us to keep the costs managed, while bringing the design closer to the look of an F1 car while enhancing the F2 car’s ability to deliver close racing.

"We have added an on-board starter that will simplify the operational side for the teams and will allow the drivers to restart their car after spinning or stalling on track, and we’ve been continuing our work with our partners Aramco and Pirelli on driver preparation, sustainability, and providing the fans with a great show.

"Our fans expect the F2 races to be highly entertaining and safe, and this new kit will deliver exactly that."

title: FIA Courts issue statement after extraordinary Flavio Briatore allegations
excerpt:
The International Court of Appeal has issued a statement following the claims made by Flavio Briatore over alleged bias from a panel member.

The FIA International Court of Appeal has issued a statement responding to the claims made of bias by Alpine executive advisor Flavio Briatore.

On Friday in an astonishing team principal's press conference, Briatore took aim at Judge Filippo Marchino, who served as a member of the panel in the ICA hearing last month brought by McLaren and Red Bull into Pierre Gasly's Monaco GP podium and penalties.

McLaren and Red Bull were protesting the stewards' decision to rescind Gasly's two five-second sanctions for pit-lane speeding after a successful right of review by Alpine, which handed him back third place. The ICA hearing ultimately decided to restore Gasly's penalties and drop him to seventh with Isack Hadjar promoted back to third.

Alpine then issued a statement, saying that whilst it disagreed with the decision, it respected it, before Briatore, in the press conference with Andrea Stella of McLaren and Fred Vasseur of Ferrari claimed one of the judges, Marchino, was biased against Alpine.

Marchino, Briatore claimed, acted like a "prosecutor" and was "very nasty", which he accepted, but what Briatore could not was his claim that Marchino held links to McLaren and thus could not be considered as impartial.

Briatore claimed that Marchino, through his One Drop Foundation in 2018, was present at an event in Beverley Hills in 2018 where McLaren Special Operations (MSO) provided cars and claimed he had a photo of Marchino with a McLaren. MSO is the road car division of McLaren responsible for the upkeep and customisation of the vehicles and is not linked to the F1 team.

In return, a furious Stella replied that the insinuation was "insulting" and warned that people making such allegations should prepare to be able to defend them.

Marchino himself has not had a right of reply to Briatore's allegations, although he has been approached by RacingNews365 with the offer of a right of response.

The ICA itself, an independent body from the FIA, has now issued the following statement in response to Briatore's allegations.

International Court of Appeal statement in full

The FIA Courts are aware of public comments questioning the independence and impartiality of the judges of the panel that decided Case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09.

The FIA Courts wish to make clear that the appointment and participation of the judges in that case, like for any other case, were conducted in accordance with the applicable FIA judicial procedures and usual practice, which are inspired by the highest standards like the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration.

All judges are elected by the FIA General Assemblies, some of them upon proposition of a group of at least five F1 teams in accordance with the FIA Statutes. They are all subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA Compliance Officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved, which is served to the parties.

At both the beginning and conclusion of the hearing, the parties were invited to raise any issue concerning the proceedings or the composition of the Court. None did so. No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the Court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.

The ICA emphasizes the importance of constituting panels with judges from different cultural and geographical backgrounds. This helps ensure that the deliberations and discussions reflect a diversity of legal traditions, perspectives and approaches, further strengthening the fairness, independence, credibility of the process and access to a fair trial.

A Court’s decision can leave room for various interpretations and comments as for its legal merits; that is fair and accepted by all the judges. The Court is confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges. The FIA Courts remain committed to the independence and impartiality of their judges and to the integrity of the judicial process.

Laurent Anselmi (President of the ICA and of the FIA Judges Congress), Rui Botica Santos (President of the IT and Vice-President of the Judges Congress), Waltraud Wünsch (Vice-President of the ICA) and Gérard Martin (Vice-President of the IT).

title: George Russell doubles down on Italian GP stance despite practice advantage
excerpt:
George Russell has reiterated that Ferrari remain the favourites for victory at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend despite his session-topping time during FP2.

The Mercedes driver ended the second practice outing marginally ahead of Charles Leclerc, hours after Ferrari topped the first practice session.

Ahead of the race weekend, Russell labelled Ferrari as the team to beat as it entered its home event with an upgrade to its engine.

After assessing the first day of on-track action, Russell has stated his view has not changed.

“Ferrari looked very competitive and they still look to be the ones to beat,” Russell said.

“We also know how strong McLaren have been recently and I have no doubt they will get themselves in the mix for tomorrow.

“We can't count out Red Bull either. It's an encouraging opening to the weekend but it's early days. Let's see what Saturday brings.”

Russell will likely not be under significant pressure from his team-mate and title rival Kimi Antonelli this weekend, as the Italian has a grid penalty for taking on a new power unit.

Having experimented with the set-up of the cars throughout the day, Mercedes trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin detailed that it will study some final data before making the call on wing levels, which is often a crucial decision around Monza.

“The track grip has been surprisingly good from the start and that prompted us to drop the wing level with George going into FP2,” he said.

“That also gave us a good cross-car compare. There is a bit of data to pick through before we make a final decision, but we've got overnight to do that analysis.

“It certainly looks tight in terms of performance; all the teams we are fighting with have shown strong pace at various times today so we're not taking anything for granted but pleased that we seem to be in the fight.”

title: Isack Hadjar thankful to Red Bull for 'even sweeter' feeling after podium decision
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has thanked for Red Bull team for its efforts in trying to return his Monaco Grand Prix podium after it took the case to the FIA's International Court of Appeal.

Hadjar stood on the podium in Monte Carlo with third place after Pierre Gasly had two five-second time penalties added to his elapsed principality race time, dropping him to seventh.

Alpine then successfully lodged a right of review into Gasly's twin pit-lane speeding penalties, promoting the Frenchman back to third, but Red Bull and McLaren then lodged an appeal with the highest legal authority in FIA-backed motorsport, the International Court of Appeal.

The hearing took place in August, with the decision handed down on Friday, that Gasly's penalties would be reinstated, thus promoting Hadjar back to third place - his first podium for Red Bull and second of his career.

Having had the experience of standing alongside race-winner Kimi Antonelli and second-placed Lewis Hamilton, Hadjar now officially has the podium recorded in the history books.

"It's great to get the podium back," said Hadjar.

"I've always said you could never take away the feeling of standing on the Monaco podium, no matter the result, but to have it officially in the record books is sweeter.

"A big thanks to Laurent [Mekies] and the team for fighting hard off-track to get this one back, my first in these colours."

title: Lando Norris addresses Ferrari 'worry' as major upgrade set for introduction
excerpt:
Lando Norris has addressed Ferrari’s second power-unit upgrade for this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix, insisting it is not something that worries McLaren.

As part of the Additional Development Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) scheme, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc will both have a new and more powerful engine.

Top speed and horsepower have been the Scuderia’s biggest weaknesses since the introduction of the new power-unit regulations, while its chassis is viewed as the best on the grid.

However, this has left Ferrari exposed at high-speed circuits, making Monza a huge test for the Maranello-based outfit.

The hope for the Italian marque will be that its new engine pushes it closer to the Mercedes power unit’s performance, with Norris expecting it to be a bigger threat from this weekend.

Asked if he is worried about Ferrari this weekend following its engine upgrade, Norris told select media, including RacingNews365: "Not worried at all. I mean, they’ve been very competitive, and it probably will make them more competitive.

"So, good on them. They’ll make my life a bit trickier. It’s clearly been their biggest weakness, I would say, in many scenarios. So they’ll become a bigger threat this weekend for sure.

"But I’m not worried. If they beat us, they beat us because they deserve to. So it’s not a worry. We have to just keep focused on our own job. We know it’s a different track.

"We know that there are still, you know, we’ve won two races, but it’s not like we’ve been competitive the whole season. And we know that there are things we still need to work on, like I’ve said many times.

"So this is a different track. We’ll be patient. We’ll see where we stand, and then we’ll give you a better answer."

title: Pierre Gasly feels 'robbed' after court decision strips Monaco podium
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly says he believes Alpine is being "robbed" following the FIA International Court of Appeal's decision to strip him of his Monaco podium.

On Friday, the FIA's ICA handed down its ruling over McLaren and Red Bull lodged a appeal against steward document 99 and decisions 1 and 2 from the Monaco GP, those which rescinded Gasly's two five-second time penalties for speeding in the pit-lane at the Monaco GP, which dropped him from third on the road to seventh.

Alpine had successfully overturned those penalties on a right of review after it was found the official timekeeper had made a mistake in measuring the length of the pit-lane, something the Monaco race stewards were not aware of when handing out the penalties to various drivers, including McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Gasly.

McLaren could not appeal Piastri's penalty as no mechanism exists in the rulebook to undo the effects of a served penalty, but Gasly did not serve his 10 seconds total penalty by stopping in the pits, with the time added to his elapsed race time, something drivers often opt to do.

After hearing the case last month, the FIA's ICA, the highest legal body it is possible to go to in FIA-sanctioned motorsport, decided to reinstate Gasly's two five-second time penalties, thus dropping him to seventh again with Isack Hadjar now third, Piastri fourth, Liam Lawson fifth, and Arvid Lindblad sixth.

Alpine had accepted the decision, before executive advisor Flavio Briatore launched an astonishing broadside attack against one of the judges on the panel and hinted that further action could be taken.

It is possible for Alpine to seek a right of review of the ICA's ruling, if evidence not available at the time of the hearing comes to light.

Reflecting on the ruling, Gasly felt Alpine was "being robbed" of its first podium since the 2024 Sao Paulo GP.

"I think we’re being robbed, and I don’t think it’s going to stop there. It was quite clear, the speed we had in the pit lane, and there are a lot of interpretations and legal battles being fought in offices over points that go beyond what happens in sport," Gasly told Canal+.

"And that is sad, to see results decided as a consequence of this kind of event.

"On track, we finished third. Then there was another twist afterwards.

"Anyway, I’ll let my team take care of the rest. I did everything I could on track, and now it’s up to them to do what’s necessary.

"I have confidence in that."

title: The secret behind Ferrari's straight-line boost at Italian GP
excerpt:
Ferrari's upgrades in Italy did not merely centre around the upgraded power unit and the modifications permitted under second phase of ADUO [Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities].

The Italian squad entered its home round as it seeks to climb onto the top step of the podium on home soil once again, having last done so in 2024.

Given the unique characteristics of this circuit, which favours aerodynamic efficiency, the Scuderia has sought to find the optimum compromise between the load generated by the bodywork and straight-line efficiency.

Straight-line speed has been a consistent weakness for Ferrari this year, and has been a point of frustration for both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at times.

At Monza, the modification made to the FTM [flick tail mode] profile stands out, as it is now made up of a wide vertical slit that effectively divides the previously single profile into two distinct sections.

The aim of this wide vertical slit is to allow the exhaust gases to flow more freely, in such a way as to exploit the intake and exhaust air pressures in favour of a, albeit slight, increase in the power delivered at the highest engine speeds.

In practice, the engineers have considered that the slight loss of downforce caused by the smaller surface area of the modified FTM is more than compensated for by the increase in PU performance on a circuit where even the smallest advantage in terms of power can provide a benefit on the long straights.

Ferrari managed to top the first practice session with Hamilton and Leclerc finishing in first and second, respectively, while Leclerc kept himself in the fight at the front once again during FP2.

Saturday's sessions will issue further clues into just how much performance the team is gaining with its upgrades - but as always, these modifications are compromise choices.

While slightly reducing the downforce generated through the main profile of the rear wing, which is partly fed by the FTM, this does not result in less rear grip, both because the downforce is reduced by very little and because, as speed increases, a high level of aerodynamic support is obtained on the rear axle.

title: Oscar Piastri navigating F1 'spiral' tightrope as ongoing struggles explained
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has explained how it is "very easy" to have a "spiral in either direction" as he tries to navigate himself out of the poor run of form in 2026.

Piastri is struggling to master the new breed of F1 car in 2026, with the cars having had their downforce slashed compared to their 2025 cousins, where the Australian led the title race for 15 rounds and won seven grands prix.

He has now gone a full calendar year since his last win, at the 2025 Dutch GP, with his struggles lying in not being able to adapt to the constant micro-corrections needed with the 2026 cars, with his driving style usually being remarkably smooth, in a clash of contrasting styles.

It is a style which suits team-mate Lando Norris, who leads Piastri by three places and 55 points in the standings, with McLaren boss Andrea Stella firmly believing that Piastri's woes are purely a technical issue as he cannot drive through "pure instinct."

After the Dutch GP, where he finished sixth, 32.332s behind team-mate Norris, who won, Piastri was determined to find answers for his poor performance, something he now believes he has, as he also offered insight into the fine line he is walking.

"Yes, I think we have. I think it's not kind of the one problem that keeps recurring; it's kind of like always chasing something a little bit different, and we need to try and find it a bit quicker, both myself and the team around me, Piastri told media, including RacingNews365, when asked if he had found answers behind his lack of pace.

"The positive from Zandvoort was that the qualifying at least looked significantly better and back to the level it should be at, and the process we're going through is just trying to extend that to the races. Obviously, the car is quite different in a race compared to every single lap, but I feel like we've got some pretty good answers to why Zandvoort, particularly, was challenging.

"We're making good progress with that. We just need time and some experimentation to find some things that are going to make us quicker. But I'm confident that we're finding the right answers and finding a way forward.

"It is not as straightforward as: 'It's just low grip.' I think this year, in particular, how I naturally like to drive a car is not necessarily the best way to drive these cars, and sometimes it has been, sometimes it's not, and I think that's going to be a little bit of the challenge.

"It's not been the same issue that we've run into every time and I think for me, it's just about trying to find that right direction, the things that make this car work, and at points we've been able to find it.

"At other points, we've tried a lot and not been able to find it. So it's not as simple as that. But when you're comfortable in the car, everything just becomes much easier.

"It's very easy to have a spiral in both directions, both a positive spiral where things feel comfortable; you've got more capacity to think about it. Everything becomes a bit more subconscious, and it just becomes easy, almost.

"Then if things aren't comfortable, you've got to think about it a lot more. You're not driving on instinct anymore, and that's why it can quite quickly unravel.

"I don't think we're at that point by any stretch of the imagination, but it's certainly not come particularly easily so far in finding solutions quickly. I think we've always kind of found solutions eventually; it's more about how we can catch things a bit quicker and adapt a bit quicker through the weekend.

"There are a lot of various things. It's not as simple as just struggling with this one thing, there are a lot of things tied up."

title: Explained: The 'bias' allegation which sparked explosive row between F1 bosses
excerpt:
What actually happened between Flavio Briatore and Andrea Stella in the Team Principals' Press Conference.

On Friday of the Italian Grand Prix, during the usual FIA Team Principals' Press Conference, Alpine executive advisor Flavio Briatore raised allegations of bias against one of the judges on the International Court of Appeal panel appointed to rule on McLaren and Red Bull's protest of Pierre Gasly's Monaco penalties being rescinded.

After Alpine had successfully lodged a right of review, it had managed to get Gasly's two five-second time penalties wiped from the record, re-promoting him into the third place he took on the road, and demoting Red Bull's Isack Hadjar to fourth and McLaren's Oscar Piastri to fifth.

McLaren and Red Bull then quickly lodged appeals against Decisions 1 and 2 of document 99 of the Monaco Grand Prix - and this was the case taken to the International Court of Appeal in Paris, on August 25th, in front of a four-person panel.

As well as those involved in the proceedings, every team was represented by an observer, with the sporting directors and general counsels making the trip to Paris, and it is made clear in the prologue of the verdict handed down that "none of the parties raised any objections, in relation either to the composition of the Court or to the manner in wich the proceedings and the hearing were conducted."

So far, so good. However, in what turned out to be an explosive press conference, Briatore made stunning claims of bias from one of the judges, but what has actually happened?

Briatore's ire during the half-hour session, in which he was grouped with McLaren’s Andrea Stella and Ferrari's Fred Vasseur, was drawn towards judge Filippo Marchion, an Italian-American, whose biography on the FIA's ICA page describes him thus.

Based in Los Angeles, an experienced trial Attorney with an educational background in Aerospace Engineering, Filippo Marchino routinely litigates some of the most technical and challenging cases in the United States.

His practice is comprised of primarily, Plaintiff catastrophic personal injury, wrongful death and complex consumer based class actions. A lifelong motorsports enthusiast, he has competed in a variety of motorsports, including currently in select events of the WRC.

When not lawyering, Filippo dedicates his time to the One Drop Foundation, which he is a Board Member of. The One Drop Foundation stands on a base of strong integrity and principles and is dedicated to bringing sustainable access to safe water and sanitation to the most vulnerable communities in the world.

The crucial point here is Marchino's links to the 'One Drop Foundation', based in California in the United States.

When invited to give his thoughts on Gasly being stripped of his podium in the press conference, Briatore, whilst saying the team respected the panel's decision, called into question Marchino's credibility and accused him of bias towards McLaren.

"This is very unfair. But you know, we accept the decision, but what is very strange was four judges in the panel. One of the judges act like a prosecutor. This is not a big problem," Briatore told media, including RacingNews365.

"The problem is he’s very linked with the McLaren company, because we have a nice picture of this guy at a speech for McLaren in 2018 in MSO, Beverly Hills. He has a foundation; it’s called the One Drop Foundation, and McLaren gave two, three McLaren cars. This was quite unfair. One of the judges was linked with a team which was processing us."

Throughout the rest of an astonishing attack, Briatore reiterated his shock at someone with apparent McLaren links being appointed to the panel judging the case, describing that Marchino had been "nasty" towards the team and acted like a "prosecutor", which Briatore had no qualms with.

But what is the reality?

Briatore claimed that he had photographic evidence of Marchino at an event in Beverley Hills for McLaren Special Operations (MSO) - the road car arm of the company responsible for the make-up and upkeep of McLaren's road cars. McLaren MSO does not, and is not linked to, the McLaren F1 Team, with them being different companies under the wider McLaren umbrella.

Marchino was not present during the press conference, nor has he had the chance to respond to Briatore's claims.

However, Stella did so and indicated that what Briatore was claiming was tantamount to libel.

"I find that this conference going in this direction is quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect," he said.

"And if anybody makes these kinds of allegations – which seem quite serious – they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

"The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal, was conducted to the highest standards, and we should not question this phase like it’s been done."

Briatore then hinted that Alpine are "thinking about what can we do next."

When approached for comment by RacingNews365 after the press conference, Alpine declined to add anything further, whilst the FIA is confident in the robust nature the ICA.
